summary: A class is the blueprint (data + methods, drawn as a 3-box UML class). An object is a specific instance created with `new`, and the variable only holds a **reference** (address) to it.
Constructors initialise objects. You can overload them, and `this(...)` chains to another constructor. `this` = the receiver object.
`rect2 = rect1` copies the reference (one object, two names). A method such as `copyObjects()` that calls `new` makes a real second object.

Accessors (get) and mutators (set) control access to private fields, and setters can validate values (data consistency). `static` = one copy per class. Class methods cannot use instance members directly.
Encapsulation vs information hiding again. Object composition ('has-a') = a field that references another object. `String` is an immutable class (reference type).
mustMemorise: UML class box: name / attributes / operations; `-` = private, `+` = public; `name: Type`, `op(): ReturnType`.
Two steps: declare `Rectangle rect;` then create `rect = new Rectangle();`. The variable stores the object's address, not the object.
Default no-arg constructor exists ONLY if you write no constructor at all.
`this(...)` calls another constructor of the same class and must be the FIRST statement.
Accessor = get (returns a field). Mutator = set (changes a field, can validate it for data consistency).
static variable = class variable: ONE shared copy. static method = class method: call it with `ClassName.method()`.
A static method cannot use instance variables/methods directly (there is no `this`). It can through an explicit object reference.
Class constant = `public static final` (e.g. `MAX_WIDTH = 100` stored as a double, prints `100.0`).
`double` always prints with a decimal point: `5.0*10.0` prints `50.0`.
Java passes everything by value. For objects, the value copied is the reference.
Naming: packages lowercase; CONSTANTS/enums UPPER_CASE; Classes/Interfaces UpperCamelCase; methods/variables lowerCamelCase.
String is a class (reference type) and **immutable**. `"Java Programming".length()` = 16, `charAt(0)` = 'J'.

items.title: Object identity
notes: Every object has its own **unique** identity (Object Identifier, OID). Two objects with equal state are still different objects.

items.title: State = attributes
notes: State is made up of attributes (properties), e.g. gender, age, monthly salary. Different objects of the same class hold different values.

items.title: Behaviour = methods
notes: Behaviour = the things an object can do. The operations an object performs are called **methods**.

items.title: UML class diagram (Person)
notes: 3 compartments: **class name** / **data (attributes)** / **methods (operations)**.
`-` = private, `+` = public. Attributes are written `name: String`, methods `eat(): void` (the return type comes after the colon).
A class = blueprint containing data properties + methods. You must define a class before you can create objects.

items.title: Class vs instances
notes: One Person class is instantiated into johnObject, billObject and obamaObject. Each has its own values for the same attributes.
Object boxes are written `objectName : ClassName` (proper UML underlines this). They show values and no methods.
The slide labels attributes + methods as 'Instance/member properties/methods', which together are the 'Class members'. These are NOT static.

items.title: Class definition syntax
notes: `public class Class_Name { instance variable declarations; method definitions; }`. `class` is the keyword. The usual order is data first, then methods.

items.title: Rectangle = abstraction
notes: Of the infinitely many rectangles, keep only the common essentials: attributes **width, height** and operations **area, perimeter**. The slide labels this 'OO: abstraction'.

items.title: Rectangle code and UML
notes: `private double width;` maps to `- width: double`. `public double findArea()` maps to `+ findArea(): double`.
Private data + public methods is labelled **encapsulation / info hiding**.
Without a constructor, the fields default to `0.0`.

items.title: Method header
notes: `public <static> Return_Type Method_Name(Parameter_List)`. `static` is optional.
The return type can be a primitive, `void`, or a class type (abstract data type). The parameter list accepts the input data.
E.g. `public static int successor(double num)` takes a double and returns an int.

items.title: Creating objects: 2 steps
notes: 1) Declaration: `Rectangle rect;` (a reference variable only). 2) Creation: `rect = new Rectangle();` allocates the object, and its address goes into `rect`.
Memory picture: `rect` (at 1024) holds **1068**, the address of the object whose data is 1.0, 1.0.
The creation line on the slide is missing the `new` keyword (the 'keyword' arrow points to the gap). It is always `= new Class_Name();`.
The 1.0/1.0 values assume the no-arg constructor from slide 19. With the slide-14 class (no constructor) the fields would be 0.0.

items.title: Reference vs object
notes: `rect` stores the **memory address** of the Rectangle object, not the object itself.
`rect3 = rect2;` copies the address, so both refer to the SAME object (2034). No new object is made.
Trap: the slide shows `Rectangle rect3;` as `null`. That is true for a **field**. A **local** variable declared without a value is *unassigned*, and reading it is a compile error.

items.title: Constructors and the default constructor
notes: Constructors initialise object data. They have the class name and **no return type**. Several constructors = **overloading**.

If you write NO constructor, Java supplies the default `public Rectangle() { }`. Once you write ANY constructor (e.g. only `Rectangle(double,double)`), `new Rectangle()` is a **compile error** (checked with JDK 17).
'Does nothing' really means: it calls `super()` and the fields keep their defaults (0, 0.0, false, null).

items.title: Constructors in UML (typo)
notes: Constructors appear in UML as `+ Rectangle()` with no return type.
The slide writes `+ Rectangle(w: double, h : height)`. It should be `h: double`. Parameters are written `name: Type`.

items.title: Calling the two constructors
notes: `new Rectangle()` gives width = height = 1.0. `new Rectangle(10.0, 20.0)` gives width 10.0, height 20.0. The arguments match the parameters by position.

items.title: Finalizer, not destructor
notes: Per the slides, Java's 'destructor' is the **finalizer**, the `finalize()` method, which releases resources. Memory is reclaimed by the **Garbage Collector**.
Real Java: there is no destructor. `finalize()` is not guaranteed to run and has been **deprecated since Java 9**. For the exam, answer 'finalize()' if asked what the slides call it.

items.title: Message sending syntax and the 'NullPointerException'
notes: Syntax: `objectRef.method(args)`, read as object reference, dot operator, method name, arguments.

The slide says `Person bill; bill.comeDown();` gives a **NullPointerException**. If `bill` is a **local** variable it is really a **compile error** ('variable bill might not have been initialized', checked with JDK 17).

You get an NPE at run time when the reference is `null`, e.g. `Person bill = null;` or an unset field. If asked 'what happens' about code, use the real behaviour. If asked for the slide's point, the answer is: the reference must refer to an existing object.

items.title: Field initialisers
notes: `private double width = 5.0; private double height = 10.0;` give every new Rectangle those starting values, even without a constructor.

items.title: RectangleApp output: doubles print .0
notes: Prints `The area of rectangle is 50.0` and `The perimeter of rectangle is 30.0`.
A `double` always prints with a decimal: `50.0`, never `50`. `(5.0+10.0)*2` is `30.0`.

items.title: Copying a reference vs copying an object
notes: `rect2 = rect1;` makes **one object, two references**. A change through rect2 is visible through rect1.
`copyObjects()` does `new Rectangle(width, height)`, a genuinely new object with the same values.

This is also how passing works: Java is **pass-by-value**, and for objects the value is the reference. A method can change the object's fields through it, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller's variable.

items.title: Two separate objects in memory
notes: `rect1` holds 1068 and `rect2` holds 2068. Each address points to its own block holding 10.0, 20.0.
Equal state, different identity. So `rect1 == rect2` is `false` (it compares references).

items.title: The keyword this
notes: `this` = the **receiver object**, i.e. the reference to the current instance the method was called on.
If you call a method or use a field without naming an object, Java uses `this` automatically, so `findArea()` means `this.findArea()`.

items.title: this for instance variables
notes: `this.width * this.height`. When `rect1.findArea()` runs, `this` holds rect1's reference. When `rect2.findArea()` runs, it holds rect2's.

items.title: Parameter shadowing and this(...)
notes: The slide says parameter names 'must not be the same' as instance variable names. Real Java **allows** it: the parameter **shadows** the field.
Bug shown: `width = width;` assigns the parameter to itself, and the field stays `0.0` (checked: prints 0.0 0.0). Fix: `this.width = width;`.
`this(10.0, 20.0);` calls the 2-argument constructor of the same class.

items.title: Constructor with this.field = param
notes: `this.width` (the field, circled) = `width` (the parameter). This is the standard Java idiom.

items.title: Constructor chaining with this(1.0, 1.0)
notes: The no-arg constructor becomes `this(1.0, 1.0);`, which delegates to `Rectangle(double w, double h)` and avoids duplicated code.
Rule: `this(...)` must be the **first statement** in a constructor, or it is a compile error (checked with JDK 17). Ch3 has `super(...)`, which follows the same rule.

items.title: Accessors and mutators
notes: Can another object change the data directly? 'NO' (well, yes if it is `public double height;`, but that is very bad OO design).
**Accessor = get method**: returns the value of a data property. **Mutator = set method**: changes the value and helps maintain **data consistency** (validation).

items.title: Full Rectangle with get/set
notes: Box 1: private data. Box 2: constructors (no-arg chains with `this(1.0, 1.0)`). Box 3: set and get methods. Box 4: other methods.
These setters do NO validation, so `setWidth(-5)` would be accepted. Slide 48 adds validation.

items.title: GetAndSetApp output
notes: Start (5,10): area 50.0, perimeter 30.0. After `setWidth(20.0)`: 200.0 / 60.0. After `setHeight(40.0)`: 800.0 / 120.0.
`print(Rectangle r)` receives a **copy of the reference**, so it reads the same object.

items.title: static = per class
notes: static variables = **class variables**, static methods = **class methods**. They apply to the whole class, not to individual objects.
There is ONE shared copy (e.g. `private static int numRectangles;`), shared by all objects of the class.
The slide says 'static instance variable', which mixes up the terms. A static field is a **class** variable, NOT an instance variable.

items.title: Counting objects with a static counter
notes: Each constructor does `numRectangles++`. After 3 `new` calls the single counter goes 0, 1, 2, 3.
Memory picture: each object has its own width/height, and the one `numRectangles` cell (4068) sits outside all of them.

items.title: Static methods
notes: `public static void setNumRectangles(int)` and `public static int getNumRectangles()` only touch static data, so they are class methods.
`private static int numRectangles = 0;` initialises the class data.

items.title: Calling class methods
notes: From outside the class: `Class_Name.Method_Name()`, e.g. `Rectangle.getNumRectangles()`. `Math` (e.g. `Math.sqrt`) is the classic example.
Calling a static method through an object reference also compiles, but it is still static (slide 56 does this).

items.title: Static cannot use instance members
notes: Class methods can use class variables and methods but **not** instance variables or methods directly.
Calling `findArea()` inside `static countArea()` is a compile error, because there is no `this` receiver.
Can you just make `findArea()` static? **No.** It uses the instance fields `width` and `height`, so it would then fail itself.

items.title: Class constants and validating setters
notes: `public static final double MAX_WIDTH = 100;` is a class constant. The int 100 is widened to double, so printing it gives `100.0`.
The setter validates: `if (w >= MAX_WIDTH) width = MAX_WIDTH; else width = w;`. So `setWidth(150)` gives `100.0` (clamped). Negative values are NOT checked.
Advantages of constants: (1) easy to change to a new value, (2) symbolic names are easier to understand.

items.title: Complete class: typo heigth
notes: Labels: class constants (per class), instance variables (per object), static variable (per class).
Typo: `heigth = h;` would be a compile error (cannot find symbol). It should be `height = h;`.

items.title: Instance vs static methods (cont.)
notes: Instance methods: `getWidth`, `getHeight`, `findArea`, `findPerimeter`. Static methods: `setNumRectangles`, `getNumRectangles`.

items.title: UsingStaticApp
notes: Static methods are called by **class name** (`Rectangle.getNumRectangles()`). Instance methods are called on an object (`r.getWidth()`).
`static print(Rectangle r)` CAN call instance methods, because it uses an **explicit reference** `r`. The 'no instance access' rule only covers implicit `this`.
`print(rect1)` is called without a class name because it is in the same class.

items.title: UsingStaticApp output mismatch
notes: The values are right: 5x10 gives 50.0 / 30.0. After set(40, 10) it gives 400.0 / 100.0. `Number of rectangles = 2`.

But slide 51's code prints `"Width = " + w + "Height = " + h`, which really gives `Width = 5.0Height = 10.0` (there is no `; `). The slide also shows 'area of **the** rectangle', which the code does not print.
Exam: trust the code for the exact text, and trust the numbers shown.

items.title: Scopes: class / object / method
notes: The outer oval is the class, holding **class (static) variables**, one copy. Each Object oval has its own **instance variables**. Each Method has **local variables**.
Class (static) methods sit outside the objects. The red **X** means a static method cannot reach into an object's instance variables directly.

items.title: Person: instance + static calculateBMI
notes: `calculateBMI()` (instance) and `static calculateBMI(double, double)` legally share a name, because their parameter lists differ (overloading).

Bug in the image: the instance method body is `calculateBMI(height, weight);` with no `return`, which is a compile error ('missing return statement', checked). It should be `return calculateBMI(height, weight);`.

items.title: PersonApp BMI output
notes: Prints `BMI is 21.604938271604937` twice (70/1.8²), then `BMI is 24.930747922437675` (90/1.9²). Checked with JDK 17.
`bill .calculateBMI(h, w)` calls the STATIC method through a reference. It is legal but misleading, and `Person.calculateBMI(...)` is the proper form.

items.title: Encapsulation vs information hiding (again)
notes: **Encapsulation**: a barrier protecting **private data**, accessed through **public methods** (get/set).
**Information hiding**: hides the **details/implementation** of the class from users.
Users know **what** the class does and **how to call** it, not the implementation.

items.title: Purpose
notes: Encapsulation and information hiding help to **protect what you have** and **protect your data**.

items.title: Interface (API) vs implementation
notes: Visible to USERS (Interface/API): **public method headers** + **public class constants** (MAX_WIDTH, MAX_HEIGHT).
Hidden (implementation): private instance variables, **private methods** (`- optimiseResult()`), and the **bodies of ALL methods, public ones included**.
Trap: a public method's *body* is still hidden. Only its *header* is part of the interface.

items.title: Object composition = has-a
notes: An object holds references to other objects as **instance variables** (data members), e.g. `private Course course;` means a Student **has a** Course.
Object references are **reference data types**.
Ch2 uses 'composition' loosely for any has-a field. In Ch6 UML, composition is the strict whole-part link (filled diamond). Do not carry the Ch2 meaning into Ch6 questions.

items.title: Course class
notes: Constructor + setters use `this.x = x`, where the parameters shadow the fields (see slide 35).

items.title: Composition in memory
notes: `myStudent` points to the Student object. Its `course` field holds a **reference** pointing to a separate Course object. The Course is NOT copied inside the Student.
The constructor parameter `Course courseIn` is assigned to `course`. The Course was created outside and passed in.

items.title: printInfo uses the composed object
notes: Student delegates to its Course through message sending: `course.getCourseId()`, `course.getYear()`, etc. It cannot read Course's private fields directly.

items.title: StudentApp: undefined type StudentInfo
notes: `StudentInfo myStudent1 = new Student(...)` does not compile unless `StudentInfo` is a superclass or interface of Student, and none is defined. Read it as `Student myStudent1`.
Each Student gets its own Course object (course1, course2, course3).

items.title: StudentApp output
notes: `Height: 1.75` (a double prints as written). `Gender: M` (a char). Course, Year, Semester and Score are ints with no `.0`.

items.title: Array of objects
notes: `private Course[] course = new Course[3];` creates an array of 3 **references**, all initially `null`. Each `new Course(...)` must still be created separately.
Picture: the Student's `course` field points to the array, and the array slots [0], [1], [2] point to the Course objects.

items.title: Database of composite objects
notes: `School` has `Student[] myStudentArray` (indices 0 to numOfStudent-1). Each Student has a `Course[]` of 3. These are references all the way down.

items.title: Data types tree
notes: Reference types = **Array, Class (e.g. String), Interface**. Primitive types = boolean, numeric (byte, short, int, long, float, double) and character (`char`).
**String is a class/reference type, NOT a primitive.** Java has 8 primitives: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean.
The slide puts char separately from 'Numerical'. In real Java `char` is an integral type (`ch++` works).

items.title: String class
notes: `java.lang.String` is a class, and strings are always objects.

`String s = new String("Java");` or `String s = "Java";`. Trap: two identical literals share one pooled object (`==` is true), but `new String(...)` always creates a new object (`==` is false, `.equals` is true). Checked.

items.title: String is immutable
notes: `aString` holds the reference address. "Java Programming" has length **16** (indices 0 to 15, the space is index 4). `aString.charAt(0)` is `'J'`.
`aString = "Java";` does NOT change the old string. It points `aString` at a NEW String object, and the original is unchanged (immutable).

items.title: Java naming conventions
notes: lowercase gives **packages**. UPPER_CASE with underscores gives **constants, enums**. UpperCamelCase gives **Classes, Interfaces**. lowerCamelCase gives **methods, variables**.
The slide says to use underscores when there are 'more than two words'. It means more than **one** word (MAX_HOURS has two words and still uses `_`).

items.title: Summary
notes: Objects have state + behaviour, and an object is an instance of a class. A class = the template/blueprint describing the state and behaviour its objects support.
